summary: Babylonia is a tense area-majority game where you draft tiles from shared face-up rows and chain them onto a hex map to build farms, cities, and monuments, all while jockeying for majority control near royal courts. It has classic Knizia tension: every tile you take denies an opponent, and the game can end abruptly once a tile stack runs dry, so timing your final moves matters as much as your placements.
praised: Deep, tense decision-making from a simple set of rules
Clever chaining/tile-drafting mechanism that creates constant blocking opportunities
Multiple viable scoring paths that reward different strategies
Strong table interaction typical of top-tier Knizia designs
criticised: Fiddly bookkeeping (court favor tiles, bull tokens, scoring tracks) that slows play
Steep rules/strategy learning curve for a first play
Sudden-death ending can feel abrupt or anticlimactic
Dry historical theme that feels pasted on rather than integrated

interaction.kind: blocking and area denial through competitive tile drafting

scoring.why: Points come from several semi-independent systems (farm/irrigation majorities, city/court favor, ziggurats, and bull-token bonuses), so the winner is whoever best balances multiple scoring engines rather than maxing one.
